utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you expanded on your opinion on Friday, you seemed to assume that the vehicle could only be seen in the space between the end of the barricade and the commencement of the building line as it travelled south down the road on which it was -- on which it was hit, that is, Ante Babica Street. Is that correct? That was the assumption that you made.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assumption was that the vehicle could not be seen. Partly because of the buildings, because this wasn't very clear and this is what I noticed on the scene, on the site. It was unclear what had been built by then and what not. So even today in a way it's hard to check this. And on the other hand, I don't know what was the height of the barricades, and I assumed when I was speaking about the assumption, about the supposition that the vehicle had been appearing behind a barricade. It was just -- whether it was hidden by buildings or barricade ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Again, if you could please focus on the question. In giving your evidence on Friday, you repeatedly referred to the time period that the building would have -- I'm sorry, that the truck would have been observed. And as I understood it, you assumed it could only be seen from the Bosnian Serb side as it passed from the end of the barricade to where it was then blocked by buildings further south. Is that correct? Was that your assumption?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also gave us some figures based on whether the vehicle was travelling at 60 kilometres an hour or 40 kilometres an hour. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in reading or having read to you the evidence given in court, did you understand firstly that the barricades were lower than the top of the truck? In other words, the barricades did not obscure entirely the truck from view.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that the barricade was high enough that you wouldn't be able to see the lorry very well immediately. I -- that was just an example. It wasn't a statement. If it had been a statement, I would have included it in my report. But it was just an example to explain how difficult it is to ascertain something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may not remember this. I wouldn't expect you to. But we've heard evidence that the truck was about 5 metres long, the cabin was separate from the back of the truck, the back of the truck was about 3 metres high, and the cabin was about 2 and a half metres high. And the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the barricade was about 2 metres high. In other words, if that evidence is correct, then the barricade did not obscure the truck. That follows from those figures, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you also discern in the evidence that was read to you a contention from the Prosecution that the student hostels at the time did not entirely block the view from the Bosnian Serb side of traffic travelling along Ante Babica Street?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on the photograph it was marked which part of the student hostel was missing. But as far as I know, there were one or two houses there or one behind another. It can be seen on a photograph. I don't know whether they existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do I take it that you don't remember being exposed to evidence to the effect that walls were missing in those buildings, allowing a line of sight through the buildings from the road to positions held by the Bosnian Serb army? Do you not remember that? For instance, the evidence given by the father who was driving the truck, to the effect that the floors were completely hollow, one could see right through them. Do you remember reading that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember all of it, yes. I remember that part. If there was a view, then of course the situation is different, if there was. But I don't know. If it was not possible to see -- this is what I listed, what the problems are, if it is not possible to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. No one expects you to draw final conclusions from those aspects of the evidence as to whether it was possible or not possible to see through the building. But in terms of preparing a -- an impartial report, it's important to take into account different outcomes, depending on different views of the evidence. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. But what I stand by, what's in my conclusion is the material traces. The statements, I have to always take --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Later. Let's stick with the issue I'm asking you about for the time being. Now, if it was possible for whoever fired that bullet to glimpse the truck making its way up Ante Babica Street heading south, up the slope, just glimpse bits of it, they could start to move their rifle in line with the truck, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object. This is purely hypothetical and subjective. The witness was not there at the time. And to know what we were -- we would have been able to see, I don't think it's possible to ask such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has testified on the basis of some assumptions. The witness has also expressed himself on the issue of how much time one would need to target, the time a bullet would need to travel. I understand the question to be in the same area, and therefore the objection is denied. But let me be on one thing quite clear: Just as you gave your expertise, starting from certain assumptions, I think neither counsel nor the Chamber expects from you to have any knowledge as what has happened at that time. You're just asked about what would be according to your expertise and your experience -- what would be possible in the circumstances as they have been presented to you. Whether these are true or not is a totally different matter. I think you very well understood this, but I just wanted to stress that again, that no one is expecting you to give information of a situation you've never seen. You were at least not present when the time -- at the time that it happened. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, what I'm suggesting is that it would be possible for whoever fired the rifle, if those floors were hollow, to glimpse the truck as it moved up the street, follow it as the top of the truck moved behind the barricade, and to be ready when the cabin window emerged from beyond the barricades. And that assumes that you couldn't see the window above the barricades. That would seem to be a possibility flowing from the evidence, just as if not more acceptable than the conclusion that you drew on Friday as to when the vehicle was visible. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, would you please go to incident 20. And again, I draw your attention to an assumption or a conclusion that you've drawn from the material that you've read. In the first paragraph, you say, "Based on the data provided by the briefs, it is possible to conclude that the victim could not have been the immediate target, that is, that no aiming could have taken place prior to firing because of the fact that the window was covered by a blind and a curtain (which made visual communication impossible)." Have I correctly read the first sentence and the first paragraph in your report of that incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in reading the evidence, did you understand that the left side of the window had glass and the right side was covered in thin plastic which allowed some light through it. There was also a blind which was holed from bullets and shrapnel. Do you remember that? If you don't remember, that's fine. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a blind, and I've stated that, that there was a curtain, plastic curtain --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can -- do you remember reading that evidence or having that evidence read to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thin plastic on the right-hand side, glass on the left, and both covered by a blind which had holes in it. Do you remember reading that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that I read it, but I don't recall things as to left and right-hand side, where was the glass and where was the plastic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No mention of a curtain though in the evidence, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's mentioned. The curtain is mentioned, as far as I recall. But I can check.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now going to the statements?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement of the husband of the injured party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dated 15th -- no, 23rd of November, 1995 -- 25th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the problem. We don't have -- we haven't been given notice of specifically which statements the witness has had access to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To whom is this statement given, Dr. Kunjadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately it has not been marked. I'll try and find it here. Yes. Here's -- here's the statement. Here is the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the statement, does it have a number or does it have -- to whom is it given?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please read the relevant part of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have to read everything. Perhaps I can use my own text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would read the literal text there where the statement deals with the way the window or windows were covered by blinds and/or curtains.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the statement be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you assist, Mr. Usher, to put the statement on the ELMO. Mr. Kunjadic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just before that happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any protective --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think that's all right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's put on the ELMO, Dr. Kunjadic, because that's easier for the interpreters to read and translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you identify the relevant spots, Dr. Kunjadic? Yes. Would you please point at it. If the usher could take care that it's entirely on the ELMO, a little bit more to the left, I would say. Yes. And could you then slowly read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The windows were covered with a green material of blind and with curtains. But now I believe that they were not sufficiently well covered. When I arrived home, I criticised them, why didn't put a blanket on the window."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So in that statement, although he refers to curtain, he also says he believes now they were not covered properly, that is, the window, and he complained at the time when he arrived home that they hadn't put up the blanket; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there's one other sentence which speaks of this. "The window closest to her still had glass, but it was covered with a blind and with curtains."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you now look further down the statement, the third-last paragraph, at least in the English text, starts off with the words "there was no shooting."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also read that out slowly, Dr. Kunjadic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the text is below: "It was very quiet --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness move the -- could the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you place the microphone in such a way that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point to where you are reading?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's too high up. If you come down to the third last paragraph, I think it's -- all right, do you see this in the statement towards the bottom: There was no shooting after that incident or before. I assume it was a murder on purpose because the shooter could see the shadow of the candle in the window." Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can leave that now. Were you also given copies of other statements by that witness which talked about the covering on the window, the statement of the 27th of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27th of June -- just a moment. I have -- it's dated 4th of September, 2000 -- no. No. 4th of September. No. I don't have that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, did you understand from the statements alone, without going to the evidence, that he did not believe the window was properly covered and at the time he was concerned that a blanket had not been put up over the window when he arrived home? Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that, because the event had already taken place. And he probably concluded that this was not covered enough, because there were curtains -- they were not stretched enough. And the shot happened. The shot was fired. So logically one could assume that something was not all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Especially, since the point of view which he formed at the time was that you needed to put up additional covering, a blanket, to make it safe; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know the quality of the curtains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the other screens on the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. And you'd not be expected to know that. But coming back to your report, you say that visual communication was impossible. Now, in compiling your report, did you allow for the fact -- I withdraw that. Did you allow for the possibility that whoever shot those bullets was deliberately shooting them at a window with light, rather than the outline of a body? In other words, shooting recklessly at the window through which some light could be seen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about the intentions, and technically it is possible to fire at a window. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However you cannot speak about the intentions, you did think it appropriate to make a conclusion as to whether this visual communication, as you put it, was possible. So what I'm doing is having taken you to the material that you were initially briefed with, as well as the evidence, pointing out to you that there were other possible conclusions; namely, that the -- it would seem that light may have been emitted from that window. Do you understand that, that that's what I'm putting to you? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could see the light in the window - and it was already at night, and this is just an assumption - then it could have been, in the vicinity. But here the indication is the fire -- the shot came from Hrasno Brdo, which is further away. And I agree that in this case it was possible to determine with precision the source of fire. It's one of the cases for which there were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll leave that. Now, you looked at the video, and did you see where the two bullet holes were, that is, the entry points, one on the window and one on the frame? I think that was indicated in -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And it seems that the fatal bullet passed through the window frame, the bottom window frame of the glass, and killed her within a matter of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lower part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And given where she was seated, the higher bullet hole would seem to have been just above where her head was. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the second hole was about 70 centimetres above that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that that first projectile couldn't have hit her. She was sitting. And the second one that passed through the wooden window frame is in fact the projectile that hit the victim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one hit her in the chest and the other came in just above her head; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 50 or 60 centimetres above her head. I don't know the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think that was above her head, but we won't be too troubled by that evidence at this stage. Did you note also from the evidence that the bullets, the two bullets, seemed to enter if not simultaneously then almost simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you make of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing spectacular. I didn't come to any spectacular conclusions. Two bullets hit the window. They could have been fired from a distance -- well, if the windows were covered, as said, then it was simply not possible to see because the distance was too great. I think they said it was about 800 metres. This distance is too great to be able to see the cover. If they were firing at some window, if there was some additional source of light and they fired at some window, well, I can't really be precise but -- I can't conclude anything in particular on the basis of two bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If the two bullets had been fired from the same weapon, a semi-automatic or an automatic, would you expect the impact to be simultaneous or would you expect there to be some discernible gap in time between the first and second bullet?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were fired in succession, then there would be a gap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long would that gap be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, but probably -- I don't know. I don't have the information. I don't know whether it would have been after three or eight seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to this question because everything depends on how the man or woman reacts with their hand on the trigger. How can one know? And if you have to wait a minute before the shot is fired, then it will be a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Kunjadic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President. Might I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, that is entirely inappropriate for Mr. Piletta-Zanin to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin gave an example which would stretch the time, which is certainly inappropriate. I think the information you were seeking, Mr. Ierace, which might have been sought in a more factual way, was how much would it take for a person who uses -- let's start with a semi-automatic rifle -- to fire two shots consequently on a same target? What's the minimum, approximately, for someone who is skilled or -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few seconds. Between five and ten seconds, if he wants to fire accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that this would not be possible one second, two seconds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to aim. When you fire from a rifle, it shakes. You have to align everything again. You have to aim Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. again. And this takes time, if you want to be accurate when shooting, unless a burst of fire is involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then you're then still talking about a semi-automatic rifle or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't establish the -- what the weapon used was. I agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking you about a semi-automatic rifle, and of course the same questions could be put for an automatic rifle but the answer might not be that problematic, and the same could be asked about a non-automatic rifle, an ordinary rifle. But you say that with a semi-automatic rifle you would need five seconds or more to fire a second shot with a -- with a reasonable, reasonable precision, precision of targeting? I'm not talking about high precision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be the minimum, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five seconds, the minimum. Mr. Ierace --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between five and ten seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With an automatic rifle, what would be the time gap between successive bullets?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, similarly if single shots are being fired --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I think that five to ten seconds has not been entered in the transcript. I apologise. Perhaps I wasn't following carefully. But that's my impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least the five seconds minimum are there, and I take it that ten seconds is not an ultimate maximum, but -- but that's what -- at least was translated to me as the words of the witness, that at least five to ten seconds. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the minimum time lapse if the rifle was automatic; in other words, the shooter simply keeps the trigger depressed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the weapon is automatic, you can fire a lot of bullets in a minute, for example, 120 bullets in a minute. But in this case, we're discussing whether the target is aimed at, as far as I have understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it unlikely that an automatic weapon could account for the two bullets in this particular case? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exclude the possibility, but I don't have an explanation. I don't have a good explanation for excluding this. It's possible in technical terms, but -- if it's technically possible, I see no good reason to exclude this possibility. Naturally I'm not referring to any particular kind of weapon. Any weapon could be the source of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, given the evidence that the bullets impacted simultaneously, that would seem to exclude a single semi-automatic weapon as being involved. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the information, on the basis of the fact, I can't say whether it was simultaneous. Do you mean that -- when you say "simultaneous," do you mean that two projectiles hit the window at the same point in time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not asking you to comment on that. Let's assume that for the sake of my question that the two bullets impacted at the same time. Assuming that, we therefore eliminate a semi-automatic -- a single semi-automatic weapon as being responsible for both bullets, do we not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the remaining possibilities are either an automatic, if it's a single weapon, or two weapons firing together; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean if two weapons fire at the same point in time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, that's possible, if they fire at the same time or if there is just a time lapse of a fraction of a second. But I can't really imagine a situation in which two bullets would be fired exactly at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you eliminate the possibility of there being a silhouette of the deceased on the blind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because I don't have the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in any event, the only possibilities, it would seem, are either an automatic firing two bullets in quick succession so that they both seemed to impact simultaneously; alternatively, two separate weapons being fired at the same moment, at the same instant. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this question because there's a third possibility, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, that's -- that's a matter for the witness. The witness can say that. And the witness is better placed than Mr. Piletta-Zanin to respond to that, being an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace presented you two possibilities and asked you whether you would agree that there were these two possibilities. Would you please respond to that question. If you see a third, a fourth, or a fifth one, you're free to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat this. It's possible for an automatic weapon to open fire in succession and then one projectile hits the window and it's followed by another projectile and the time lapse is minimal. In theory, it's possible for two weapons to fire at the same time and to hit a given target. In theory it's possible. Whether it's possible in practice it's really difficult for me to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you think of any other scenario that could give the same result?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not imagining various kinds of scenarios, but this is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you have your photographs with you, the ones that you showed us on Friday? No, I'm sorry. I apologise. Not in relation to this incident. On Friday you showed us a bundle of about 50 photographs that you had taken yourself in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please take out the photographs which have marked on the back numbers "20" and "21." They're the photographs of the -- the railings, I think in Dobrinja, the railings on the bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps they can be both placed on the ELMO. I think they're small enough that both could fit on at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please assist the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kunjadic. Yes, that's good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are these photographs taken of the railings on the bridges going over the Dobrinja River?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And on each of the bridges there are similar railings? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same bridge. But yes, they are similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you say -- all right. Now, which particular bridge is this? Is this the bridge for incident number 6?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the bridge where the bicycle incident occurred. Which one was it? I think it's the -- I think it's in Nikola Demonija Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's further to the south from incident number 6, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incident number 6 is downstream. It's further down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Downstream the Dobrinja River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these bridges -- I'm sorry, the railings, did you examine them closely?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. But I can see that these are the projectile impacts. That's why I took these photographs. When this happened, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you took these photographs pointing downstream or pointing upstream, or is one taken one way and the other one the other way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's another photograph that was taken from this bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you: Is the lower photograph a part of the upper photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But it's taken from closer up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From closer up. The same position. Yes, please. Thank you. It was just for myself to better understand the testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you find a third photograph? I think you were looking at the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for the third photograph. But you can see that it's the same photograph because of this building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's larger here, and it's smaller in this place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time you took these two photographs, were you facing upstream or downstream?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both upstream and downstream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was taken downstream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking downstream; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Downstream. Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before you go to the third photograph. In relation to the two in front of you at the moment, were you facing downstream when you took them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at the third photograph. Do we see the railing in the third photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll take that one away for the moment, please. All right. Now, coming back to the other two. Do you agree with me that when one examines those railings closely, there are a far greater number of impacts on the sides of the railings which face upstream than there are on the sides of the railings which face downstream?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words -- I withdraw that. Now, do you also agree with me that when you examine those railings closely, some of the bullets are seen to penetrate both skins --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we zoom in to the extent that this is possible so that we can verify what Mr. Ierace means when he says "upstream and downstream." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you: You were asked about impacts on the railings facing upstream and downstream. Could you for our convenience and to better understand your testimony indicate where you see those parts of the railing facing upstream and where you would see those parts facing --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I think the problem lies in my question. I may have misled the witness. I'll clarify that question. I'll go back to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking about what we see in these -- in this particular railing in these photographs. Do you understand? I'm asking you about observations that you made on the railings on the bridges crossing the Dobrinja River when you visited Sarajevo. Do you understand my question? Well, do you understand the basis of my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as a result of your observations and leaving aside what we see on the particular railing at the moment, do you agree that there are more impact points on the sides of the railings that face upstream? In other words, that are exposed to the south. I'm not asking you about what we see on this -- on these particular two photographs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There are more impacts on the sides of the railings which face the south compared to the sides of the railings which face the north. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we ask this question, I'd like to see if the witness could take the same type of photograph from the other side to examine this before we contest the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Dr. Kunjadic: Have you taken photographs of the other side of the railings, or did you just photograph this side of the railings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only photographed this side and this side of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your testimony was that you took these photographs in order to have a picture of the impacts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I remind you that some of your interruptions, objections, have a tendency of influencing the witness. You should be very careful with that. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me there are more impacts on the sides of the railings facing south, that is, upstream, compared to the sides of the railings facing north, that is, downstream?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you -- when one examines the railings, especially on this particular bridge which appears in the -- on the screen at the moment, do you agree that there are some bullet holes or holes which penetrate both skins of the railing? The railing did not stop them. They passed right through the railing. I'm not suggesting that we can see some of those on these particular photographs, but rather, when there, one can see such holes going all the way through.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not to be excluded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you form a view as to what the -- the horizontal bar of this particular railing was made from? What material was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't that interested in this. It was just something I had observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question is whether you know what the material was of which these railings were made, whether it was of specific interest to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A metal railing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that not only is it metal but it's very thick metal, in the order of in imperial measurements about a quarter of an inch for each skin. Would you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise. I think it's too thick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, too thick for what? Do you mean that the thickness I suggest to you is inappropriately thick?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my assumption. But I really don't know much about railings and how railings are made. But I think a quarter of an inch is too thick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not sure whether the witness knows what a quarter of an inch means exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness doesn't know, he'll certainly ask Mr. Ierace. I take it that if you do not understand a question to the full extent, that you'll be cautious enough to ask for further explanation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll then -- we'll now adjourn for 20 minutes. There might be some more questions for you, Dr. Kunjadic, after the break. But I'm certain that we'll finish by today. We'll adjourn until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom. Is there any need to re-examine the expert? Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon again. And I'd like to come back to some of the things that you answered. In relation to what you stated on page 8, 10 or 11 today, in relation to a curve of a shot, you say that if we have two points- one point of impact and one of penetration - that it is possible to reconstruct -- or to find the source of fire. But you say that the trajectory is not a straight line. That's what I understood that you said. Could you please give us more precision on this statement. When we are talk about great distances, does this change anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Re-examination does not, in my respectful submission, entitle one to revisit the subject matter, because it came up in cross-examination. There has to be some clarification that's required. And the witness was asked quite comprehensively in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll deny the objection, since it took me too much time up till the moment where I thought I understood exactly what the expert witness said. So I think there is a need here to avoid whatever confusion as to the exact meaning of the testimony of the witness. Please proceed. But let's just start with what the witness said, that is, on shorter distances that the line would be approximately a straight line. And I understood that exactly in relation to the questions -- questions about where a projectile would, for example, enter into a building and then through a window or through whatever and then would at a short distance - and I understand that it's within 5 to 10 metres. That's how I understood your testimony - would then impact on, for example, a wall. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see the witness is nodding yes. The interpreters cannot translate your nodding, so I would invite you to speak in words rather than -- to affirm your nodding. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But so that the Defence can understand perfectly:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, a long-distance shot implies, of course, a trajectory which is not a straight line but that it is probably a curved line. Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, witness, that there were tables. I think these are technical tables that you spoke about. Do these tables allow you to make calculations of a -- the way the trajectory descends and the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the curve as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From all the scenes that you saw in Sarajevo, on some cases this is possibly -- I mean, the cases you have analysed -- have you made my reference to these scientific tables?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in relation to expert analysis, and it's not in connection to the on-site investigation itself. But there are no data from the on-site investigations that would allow us to make this analysis, to use these tables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But when these investigations have been conducted, in some incidents we have two points in order to determine the direction -- have you found any trace of a reference to these tables in order to ascertain the height of the point of firing if we have in front of us a hill?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your knowledge, would it have been useful to refer to such tables?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as I have said, there are no -- there's no data, so nobody could have used any kind of tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just interfere to see whether we can clarify the issue. Is it true that these tables are assisting in calculating the direct -- the trajectory of a projectile if you know at what angle it's fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you know the angle of impact, that is, the angle where the -- where there is the impact, that is the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is a larger angle than the one from where the shot was fired. So they would -- those -- those two -- from the size and the data and according to the assessment of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. energy, it would be possible with a high probability to determine the location from where -- from which the shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would need the characteristics of the -- of the shell as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. These data are missing in all these case, as far as I understand. Both the angle and the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in all of the cases. There is one case, and we processed it here, where there is a projectile where the points -- I'm talking about case number 27 -- where we also had the projectile and we had the points. And if all this had been done properly, we would have certainly had a part of the trajectory. We would have been able to assess where the shot was fired from. In that case, we had the data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But also the -- did you also have the exact data of the -- I would say the propulsing power of the -- of the shell used, the -- how do you call it? The cartridge? Would you need that or -- to come to final conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I would -- in order to identify the projectile, you'd need to establish the calibre and the mass, the volume of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'd like now to go to the incidents that we spoke about. That's on page 18. And you were asked a question about the impossibility to conduct an investigation through a reconstruction in a surroundings where there is exchange of fire taking place. Now, if these investigations had been redone hypothetically through a reconstruction, a fortnight, a month, two months later, while the traces were still visible, that would have been useful in order to ascertain scientifically the origin of fire, the type of injury, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please refrain from leading, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. But the question may be answered because the -- So the question was, Dr. Kunjadic: If after a certain period of time and if some traces were still there, what -- in what way could an investigating -- an investigation at such a later date, what could it result in? What would you have been able to do? Including a reconstruction -- no, you said it was impossible. But what could be achieved after the time mentioned by Mr. Piletta-Zanin by a further investigation, traces still being there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be possible to fix these traces as if an investigation had been carried out, particularly for enclosed spaces where you have damage done by projectiles. You can make a sketch and take all the measurements that are needed for ascertaining the part of trajectory which had -- which was in that, say, apartment, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about incident 2, 3, 4. And at some point you spoke about incident number 1. But can you tell us about number 1. Did you examine it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a question far too vague, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If you want to know whether the witness has been -- what could you tell us about incident number 1 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will go to another question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incident number 4, witness. You mentioned following a Prosecution question, you mentioned some people and some statements. In relation to this incident, have you examined or looked at other statements apart from those that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the entirety of the material, and I mentioned this in the working version, whose statements I had taken into consideration. Of course, in the working version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my question is the following: You mentioned some statements, some official statements. In relation to this incident, did you examine other statements apart from those that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which ones you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. As I do not wish to lead, I will not ask this question because I can see what's going to happen. I'm going to pass on to other questions. You were asked a question of a bullet marked as "S," S-bullet. Can you tell us, as an expert, are there any S-bullets that would be different through their -- in terms of their quality if we are looking at the bullets of the same calibre but if they do not have this marking "S," S-marking?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The marking "S" is engraved on the cartridge of a 7.62 bullet times 54. Such ammunition is used by snipers. When the bullet is fired, that is, towards the place that is going to -- is hit, the projectile arrives at that place. When you look at this projectile, 7.62 times 54, you cannot establish which one it is because the same type of projectile is used by machine-gun M-84, except that its ammunition does not have this S-engraving, which is on the cartridge of the S-bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Witness, what about the charges, the gunpowder that's in the charge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Characteristics of this bullet is that the range is 3.800 metres. It can hit -- it's -- it is effective at about one-third of that range. It can hit and kill almost at any point in the trajectory. This bullet is stronger than 7.62 times 39, which is used by automatic and semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have spoken about incident number 6. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that you had filmed a video at that location.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the same as for incident number 5.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about this incident. Why did you shoot that video when we speak about incident number 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The relevant evidence by the witness is on page 13 at around line 18. The information as to why he filmed it is contained there and was not responsive to the question asked of him. If one looks at the question preceding the answer and the question immediately after, I think that is clear. And, therefore, there is no proper basis to go further into that issue arising from cross-examination. This was a video which the Defence had during examination-in-chief. They disclosed a copy to us last week. If they wanted to get into that, then examination-in-chief was the time to do it. And if you're against me, Mr. President, I'd seek leave to cross-examine the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if there was any -- we haven't seen that video. The Prosecution has not asked about the reasons, although some information might have been given. What would be the need at this moment to enter that area in response to what happened in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot say this in front of the witness, and looking at the time perhaps -- but perhaps I can do it at a later stage. But if we have to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said asked by the Prosecution and you were interrupted about an intentional nature of a shot, you said that you could not rule that out. Now, my question is the following: In relation to a shot, would it be possible, when we don't know who fired the shot, would it be possible to rule anything out? That is, would it be possible that this was intentionally done or that this is an accident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as intentions are concerned, I never stated anything about in any of the cases. I -- only about technical possibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, it seem that is you were reproached on several occasions you went past the site of incident number 11 and that you did not try to find out about such-and-such a house. But in any case, did you find in the file a smallest element which would allow you to ascertain exactly which -- exactly at which location the victim was at -- situated when she was hit?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Firstly, I don't know the evidence is that he drove past on several occasions. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think his clear testimony was that he did once.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And secondly, the witness has been asked comprehensively about what he had available to him on that one occasion in order to locate the position. So again, I respectfully submit there's no basis for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness stated that he went on several occasions -- went past this area on several occasions. And now the Prosecution reproached him that he didn't look at the location properly and precisely. But what I want to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, I won't do anything. Next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Prosecutor did not reproach him, but what the Prosecutor did is ask him whether he went there. Please mind your words. It's not a matter of - and I think the Chamber is in full control that no one here blames witnesses or experts for anything. It has not been done and it will not be allowed to be done. Similarly, the parties should refrain from blaming each other from things that did not happen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. May I just say that when you intervene and when I have my headphones, I cannot -- I cannot immediately react because I still have two interpretations in my ears. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in this incident and in relation to this, would it have made a difference to know where exactly the location of the incident was? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was absolutely necessary to know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Like for the other incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So since you received no indication, you couldn't really come to any serious conclusion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But I came to a conclusion on the basis of what I had at my disposal. I simply stated that it wasn't possible to determine the direction from which the projectile came and what kind of projectile inflicted the wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I would like to now turn to incident number 13. You were asked whether you were provided with the information regarding the fact that some buildings no longer had walls or windows and it was possible to see through them. Do you remember this? I'm talking about the students' hostel in particular.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, my question is as follows, and could you please focus on it: If, as has been affirmed, one can see through a building and as a result see the target on the other side, why in your opinion doesn't one attack the target if one can see it and why would one attack behind the barricades if one can't see it, if there are any reasons for this? Have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you, any reasons known to you within your expertise. If there would be any reasons out of that, please say -- tell us what expertise you would then rely upon. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the particular case, I don't know what could have been seen through a building or what could not have been seen. In relation to that incident, I provided an example. If it couldn't be seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Facts. But the question was: If you could see through a building and you could see the target on the other side - the other side of the building, I take it - why one does not attack that target. That was the question. Whether there would be any reasons not to attack the target. And I added that I would like to know your answer in view of your expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that the question is not quite clear to me and I can't answer just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please keep in mind that I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you first please put your microphone on. And then -- you took your earphones all. I hope that doesn't prevent you from hearing me. The last question, please reformulate it in such a way that you bring it within the scope of the expertise. We are not talking to a psychologist but we are talking to a ballistic expert. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to focus on the question as a ballistics expert. If I can see a target that I am going to aim at, even if this is through a building, can you think of a reason for which I'd not be able to attack, that is to say, hit this target, in ballistics terms? Technically speaking, can you imagine such a reason?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can see the target, if it's a vehicle -- if you can see this through the building, the reason for which you would not fire at it is that it is mobile, the target is mobile. When you see it and you try to fire at it, by that time the vehicle has already moved. And so in order to hit the vehicle, it is necessary to see it, in inverted commas, in time; that is to say, you have to take into consideration the movement of the vehicle and you have to ensure that the bullet and the vehicle coincide. If you don't see the vehicle, if you only see it for a short period of time, you can't fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, I'll ask you another question: When you went to Sarajevo, did you go to the area that one calls the hospital for blind children? I think that's what we call it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you investigate whether there were lines of fire, theoretical lines of fire, from this area --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll move on to another question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, to the extent that you know something about this, are there any tables for night vision -- no, whether there are any tables, for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are tables for a passive sight for firing at night, and these are used for firing at distances of up to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. I would like to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. It doesn't arise from cross-examination whether there are tables for a passive sight for firing at night. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It exists. I'll say this. If the witness would leave the courtroom, I would say why. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is that it does not derive from the cross-examination. Could you, to start with, indicate where tables for optical sight to be used at night are -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I say that I never spoke about optical sights for night, that's a translation error. I only spoke about tables. And if I express myself, I am reproached for having expressed myself in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If your question has been wrongly translated and you're the only one who could check that, I take it -- I didn't listen to your question in French. Please then put it in such a way that it becomes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I immediately said -- I drew the attention of the Serb booth that we weren't speaking about sights. I said we were speaking about table, not about sights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then indicate where tables of this kind were used in the examination-in-chief. Is it about tables of weapons or tables -- if it's not tables of sight, what are you referring to exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not say that the Prosecution had spoken about tables. What I said is that the Prosecution spoke about the light of candles. We think that there are tables which allow one to know at what distance in night the human eye can perceive the light of a candle, and this is the type of question I wanted to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin would like to know whether you are aware of the existence of tables that establish what you -- the human eye could see at night.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is information as to what can be seen and heard at night, but I misunderstood Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I thought he was talking about the existence of special tables of some kind. But in the literature you can read -- it say that is the light of a candle can be seen at a distance of 300 metres. And for example, that a man can be distinguished from a vehicle at a distance of 1.000 metres. I have this information somewhere here. I think I have a sheet of paper that says what can be seen and what can be heard at certain distances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say there is scientific information as to possibility for the human eye to discern at a certain distance certain objects. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this. It's interesting that the witness happens to have this with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And he's asked about it for the first time in re-examination. The witness was not asked in cross-examination about distances in order to view candlelight. There is no mention of it in his report. This is the new element. And if, in my respectful submission, the Defence is permitted to adduce this - and I note it's already adduced - then I seek sufficient time to prepare further cross-examination with the assistance of a Prosecution expert to properly ventilate this issue. Mr. President, that's the only way in which the Prosecution cannot be caught by surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This arises directly from the questions put by the Prosecution. The Prosecution asked whether a certain shot could be intentional. We're trying to answer this question. The first thing that comes to mind is to know at what distance one can see or not see something. And if it's no longer possible to see at distances over 300 metres, then the matter of intentionality has been solved. And if this witness can answer this question immediately and say that he knows of the existence of tables, he should tell us about it and then we will have finished with this matter. May I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this witness is a ballistic expert, and he showed that he knows of the existence of, as you said, tables and as his answer was, that there is information from literature that the limits of what a human eye or a human ear can perceive is -- has at least been the subject of research. If it's at this global level, you may ask one or more questions to this witness. But the Chamber, having looked at the curriculum vitae of this witness, cannot expect this witness to say anything about, for example, what someone of 18 years could see compared to someone who is 60 years, that -- what -- well, there are a lot of questions -- we're now dealing, as a matter of fact, with the capability of the human body, which is as far as the Chamber understands - but please correct me, Mr. Kunjadic, if I am wrong - is not the expertise of this witness. So asking him whether he heard about the existence, fine. Then we know that this is a field that could be -- could have been explored by the parties, but not in further detail and not asking him to draw conclusions on the basis of expertise which is not his. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll go to the crux of the matter immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, for the eye that sees most accurately, would it be correct to consider that the light of a candle can't be distinguished at a distance of about -- can't be made out --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I asked you to remain within the -- within the expertise of the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. And one of the things I referred to as an example was that the variety, for example, might not be in the expertise of this witness. You already answered the question that -- you talked about 300 metres. Do you have any specific knowledge as to what range is reflected by this average? Would you know what young strong eye would see still at five, six hundred metres and an old eye that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is fatigued would see? Do you have any specific knowledge on that issue, apart from the average you just gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any particular information. Obviously a young person has sharper vision than an old person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this what you assume just as I would assume it, or is it based on specific knowledge? Is it the general knowledge that younger people perform in many respects physically better than older people, or is there any specific information available to you that would allow you to support this conclusion? Because I would incline to say the same, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's nothing particular I'm referring to. It's on the basis of my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked a series of questions about impacts and the simultaneous nature of these impacts in relation to the window that we're discussing now, and you said there were two possibilities. My question is as follows, and there are two parts to my question: Is it possible that a bullet could theoretically speaking split into two parts, as a matter of principle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And as a result, is it possible for a bullet after having hit a first obstacle, is it possible for it to split into two parts and to simultaneously hit an object? Not as a bullet. Is it possible for these two fragments to hit separately the same object but at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the interpreters and the technicians. I think the Judges would not need much time. If -- I think seven to ten minutes would be sufficient. Would it be possible to continue for another 10 to 12 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That's no problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Dr. Kunjadic, we'll try to finish today. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: On Friday we saw a videotape on incident number 2, and in that videotape the OTP investigator point to four or five places where traces left by the bullet in the wall can be seen, even after the repair of the -- of the wall. My question is: Is it possible to draw conclusions from that fact, the fact that there were four or five different places in the same wall with traces of the -- of the bullet?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an on-site investigation had been carried out, then I would have known about that for sure. But if - and I'm speaking in purely theoretical terms - if four or five impact points have been identified, this could mean that this was caused by fragments of a projectile, if what the investigator pointed to when testimony was being given and if it concerns what he marked at the bottom of the wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you recall whether in that incident -- I think it was a wound in the leg of the -- of the girl. The bullet went -- entered and went out without hitting the bone? Do you know that? Or the bullet hit the wound -- the bone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't hit the bone. But when I explained the incident, I said that I didn't know the point of entry. I didn't know at which point the bullet entered the leg, whether it was from the external side or whether it was perhaps from right to left or -- or whether it was lengthwise. The precise location wasn't known. Although, this was possible. It could have been determined because there are scars on the leg for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: After watching the videotape, you don't know and you cannot draw conclusions about the type of wound. I mean if it was caused by the bullet or by a fragment of a bullet.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether it was a bullet or the fragment of a bullet. I've also spoken about this. But the information is simply insufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. The first one is: In the report I repeatedly see that you take it that a fact results from what you read or what you have seen on videos. For example, sometimes you say we don't know where the bullet came from but from what direction it came -- well, you -- at least you seem to accept that. And then in your conclusions, you do not repeat that it can be concluded that the bullet came from that direction but you would in your conclusion then write, for example, "I cannot draw any conclusions as to the origin, the position from where the fire came." Do I have to understand your report in such a way that if, for example, you say -- let me just try to find an example. In, for example, incident number 13, you say, "Only the side from which the projectile flew in can be determined." Then in your conclusion I do not find that repeated.
