Do I have to understand that where you say "only the side from which the projectile flew in can be determined" and if you do not come back to that in your conclusion, that your expertise would neither give support nor would it exclude the correctness of what earlier has been described as a possibility or what was the case? Is that a correct understanding of your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify this. What could be determined and what I accepted was the side from which the projectile was fired. But in my conclusion, I'm talking about the precise location from which the projectile was fired. So I confirm that it was from that side, but the precise location can't be determined. And that is the case for all the incidents. I don't deny that it came from a certain direction, but if I had several points I could determine the exact direction. But if I only have one point, as in this case, in the case of the vehicle, then you can only speak about this in rough terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. But even these rough conclusions are not contained in the part of the report where you say "Conclusions." You also could have written, for example, that it could not be established where the bullet came from apart from that it must have come from, well, let's say -- north -- northern direction or from south to south-west. I mean, you do not repeat these -- these facts which you seem to accept as being true or probably be true. You do not repeat them, and you now tell me that you nevertheless would accept them, although they do not appear in your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a manner of writing. I think that's what it has to do with. When I talk about identifying a location, I'm thinking about a precise location, which is why I didn't mention the side from which the shot was fired in my conclusion. That is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would have found specific reasons why it could not have been true that it came from a certain direction, would you have mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then I have one other question for you: There has been a lot said about curtains, blinds which would cover a window. And when confronted with the testimony of not having put the blanket in place, you said that it would be possible that logically one could have concluded from the incident that had happened that it had not been enough and that, therefore, blankets should have been in place. If I would confront you with evidence which says that the blanket in that month would be as a general rule -- be put in that place and not just after the incident, would you agree with me that this assumption that someone might have said something about a blanket after the incident had happened as a logical conclusion of the event would be beyond your expertise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my last question is: You told us that a bullet could split in, for example, two parts. What would be needed to have a bullet split in two parts? Would it need to impact on something, or could it just during its flight split into two parts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to hit something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has to hit something. Thank you very much for your answers. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Very quickly, some questions arising out of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you're also going to ask the interpreters for their cooperation. Let's try to keep it as brief as possible. Further cross-examination by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about incident number 2. When a bullet impacts on brick or even plaster, in your experience does it sometimes not leave a neat hole the size of a bullet but crack off an area of brick or plaster? Does that sometimes happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise but how does that stem from your Chamber's questions regarding incident number 2? Or perhaps I don't understand anything any more, which is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are referring to one of the questions of Judge Nieto-Navia?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Could you answer the question. So the question was whether impact on plaster or brick would create not a bullet-size impact but a wider area cracked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depends on the energy of the projectile itself, whether -- if it goes into plaster, that's softer, and obviously there will be damage, if it has strong energy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the question asked of you by the Presiding Judge. When a bullet splits into two, having hit something, is there a loss of energy? And if so, is it substantial?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to assume how much will be lost, but certainly some of the energy is used for the fragmentation of the projectile, if it divides into two, fragments into two. It's hard to say. It depends from which distance the projectile is fired. But certainly it loses some of its energy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware from the material you read that the bullet -- one of the bullets that entered the room travelled through not only the glass but also an internal wall and ended up in the hallway outside the apartment? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would that indicate the bullet still had considerable energy after it had entered the apartment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that in turn mitigate against the possibility of it in fact being a matter of one bullet which had split into component parts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just add, in this incident we had the jacket and parts of the projectile that were what the technicians found. And on the basis of that, we could have established whether it was one or more projectiles. But because perhaps -- because of the damage, the projectiles may not have been -- the calibre may not have been clear. But if they were picked up, then that would have added to the theoretical explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for your answers. Dr. Kunjadic, this -- Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think you didn't ask us whether your questions also raised questions for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I addressed the parties in -- but perhaps not. If not, please then proceed. Could you do this as quickly as possible though.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions as such, but I have an observation to make, in the sense that this witness told us that there were tables and that he -- he looked at those tables -- he testified about the tables at length. And perhaps we could have a look at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the tables and copies of tables so that they can be tendered and added to the file. That will certainly be important evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exculpatory evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Unless the witness is reproduced for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think as a matter of fact that -- Dr. Kunjadic, these tables of ammunition, they're generally publicised, aren't they, available by books and -- well, I see that you're referring to books, so it's not something that -- these tables are commonly available for -- Let's -- we haven't got the tables. We can't put any specific questions at this moment, I would say, on this subject. I think comments on whether the parties would try to seek these tables and what they could conclude from that in the specific incidents, that's not something, I think, that should be raised at five minutes past 2.00 for the first time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President, again I was misunderstood. I never spoke about ammunition tables but optical tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Optical tables? You mean again -- you're referring to tables -- the reason why I was then misinterpreting you: At an earlier occasion, when you said "tables," I corrected you to the sense that I said that the witness said that there was literature available which would give us information about what the human eye could see. I didn't hear him talk about tables, as a matter of fact, though your questions was about tables and the witness used totally different words. We also established, I think, that this is not the expertise of this witness. And of course, if it would be of any specific help in the presentation of the case or in rebuttal evidence to look at these tables, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- We could deal with that at a later stage. But we don't have to do it, I would say, in the presence of this witness. Then Mr. -- I take it then that you have no further questions, Mr. Piletta-Zanin -- or at least no questions, I should say. Dr. Kunjadic, this concludes your testimony in this court. It was a long way to come here. The Chamber noticed that you have been very cooperative in providing even information you used by -- when preparing your own report and made it available to both parties. I thank you very much for having answered all the questions, both of the parties and of the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher. We'll deal with the documents, if any, especially the MFI documents at a later stage. We'll adjourn until Wednesday morning at 9.00 presumably in this courtroom. Because of the schedule still to be made, I would like the parties to make themselves available so that we know about translation, expert witnesses, and long-distance witnesses, that there -- that there will be no confusion about what will be the order. If there would be any need to verify this, please get in touch with Ms. Tournaye. Yes, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
